blocks.md: A commuting zone is an area where people both live and work — a local job market. It is built by grouping counties so that most people who live in the zone also work in it. A big city and its suburbs form one zone; a cluster of rural counties around a market town forms another. Because workers rarely commute across zone boundaries, a shock that closes factories in one zone hits that zone's workers and barely touches the next. That makes commuting zones a natural unit for studying how local shocks, such as import competition, affect jobs and wages.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.md: Regional studies need units that match real labor markets; states are too big and cities leave out the countryside.

A commuting zone (CZ) is a set of counties grouped by the strength of county-to-county commuting ties, so that commuting within the zone is common and commuting across zones rare. Together, the zones cover the entire territory.

| | Commuting zone | Metropolitan area | State |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Based on | Commuting flows | Urban core and its commuting ring | Political boundaries |
| Covers rural areas | Yes — the whole mainland | No | Yes |
| Matches a labor market | Closely | For urban areas only | Poorly (several markets per state) |
| Number (US) | 722 in the standard scheme | ≈ 380 metro areas | 48 mainland + DC |

blocks.title: Beyond the lecture
blocks.md: The standard 722 zones were defined from 1990 commuting data (Tolbert and Sizer) and harmonized over decades so that census data from 1970 onward can be mapped consistently.

- Treating a commuting zone as a city: many are rural.
- Assuming no mobility: workers can migrate across zones over time; a regional analysis assumes this is slow or costly.

- Labor and trade: local labor-market effects of import competition, automation and immigration ([Shift-Share Exposure](note:shift-share-exposure), [Shift-Share Instrument](note:shift-share-instrument)).
- Urban: how skills, occupations and wages differ with city size and density.
